holidays.name: National Fruitcake Day
holidays.description: This is a day for the dense, boozy, candied-fruit loaf that people love to joke about. Some people eat it, some regift it, and a few people love it sincerely. Slice it thin and enjoy it with coffee, or use it as a doorstop.
holidays.origin: It's an unofficial food observance. It falls just after Christmas, when leftover fruitcakes are still around.
holidays.funFact: Fruitcake has a reputation for lasting a very long time. Soaking it in spirits helps preserve it, and some families keep a slice for a year and eat it the next Christmas.

holidays.name: Make Cut-Out Snowflakes Day
holidays.description: Grab some paper and scissors, fold, snip and unfold. Every flake comes out as a one-of-a-kind piece of winter art. It's a cheap, cozy way to fill a post-Christmas afternoon and decorate the windows.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial craft observance. Its origin is unclear, but it fits the winter season.
holidays.funFact: Real snowflakes have six sides or points. Most paper snowflakes are folded in a way that gives them eight, so many of them aren't accurate.

holidays.name: Howdy Doody Day
holidays.description: This day honors the freckle-faced marionette who starred in a hit children's TV show. It's a nostalgic salute to early television and the 'Peanut Gallery' of kids who cheered him on.
holidays.origin: It marks the anniversary of the show's debut on NBC. The program began airing in December 1947.
holidays.funFact: Howdy Doody had 48 freckles, one for each US state at the time. The show was one of the first big hits of early children's television.
